analysis.one_liner: Limits drug companies' legal tools for delaying cheaper generic competition.
analysis.headline: The bill won a favorable committee report in June 2003, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a generic drug company challenges a brand-name drug's patents, the brand company can use several legal moves that push back the day the cheaper copy reaches pharmacies. This bill would cap those moves: brand companies would get only one 30-month delay per challenge, generics could sue to clear bad patents, and the first generic company would lose its exclusive marketing window if it sat on the approval or cut a deal with the brand company that antitrust regulators found illegal.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, insurers, and government health programs that pay for prescription drugs. Cheaper generic versions would reach the market sooner, because brand-name companies could not repeatedly use the 30-month patent-suit delay or pay the first generic applicant to stay off the market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and health plans paying drug bills

how_it_helps.text: Brand-name manufacturers would be limited to a single 30-month stay of generic competition per patent challenge, and later-added patents would not generate new 30-month delays [S2][S3].

Generic applicants could sue for a court ruling that a patent is invalid or not infringed if the brand owner does not sue within 45 days, and could counterclaim to force corrections to overstated patent listings [S2][S3].

A first generic applicant would forfeit its 180-day exclusive marketing window if it failed to market the drug, abandoned the application, or entered an agreement with the patent owner that the Federal Trade Commission determined violated antitrust laws — a direct attack on settlements that keep generics off the market [S2][S3].
The FDA could accept alternative, scientifically valid ways to prove bioequivalence for drugs not absorbed into the bloodstream, opening more drugs to generic copies [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose patents would be litigated faster and whose ability to extend monopoly pricing through repeated delays and paid-off generic settlements would shrink.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes tools patent holders consider legitimate: a 30-month stay exists so a patent owner can defend a valid patent in court before a copy is sold, and limiting it to one per challenge means some genuinely contested patents could be decided with less full adjudication before the generic launches [S3].

The bill does not directly lower any price — it only changes the legal rules around generic entry, so any savings depend on generic companies choosing to bring challenges, and on courts resolving them quickly [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The mechanics target well-documented delay tactics, and generic competition reliably lowers what patients and insurers pay for the same medicine. The cost is borne almost entirely by brand-name patent holders through faster and narrower litigation, not by patients. The main honest caveat is that the bill is indirect — it changes legal incentives rather than setting prices — so its benefits depend on generic firms acting on the new openings.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate health committee approved it favorably one day after it was introduced, but the Senate never took it up, and it expired at the end of the Congress in January 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. Judd Gregg introduced the bill on June 10, 2003, with three Senate cosponsors, and it was referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S1][S5].
The next day, June 11, 2003, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment [S5].
No further action was ever recorded; the bill never reached the Senate floor and died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers kept their existing tools for delaying generic competition — the 30-month stays and the settlement practices the bill would have curtailed — and consumers did not get the earlier generic access the bill promised.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican sponsor with three Democratic and one Republican cosponsor, and the Republican-chaired committee reported it favorably — but the record shows no floor vote, so the shape of any opposition was never tested in a roll call.

industries.note: The bill would have cut off repeated 30-month delays of generic competition and let courts void settlements the FTC finds anticompetitive, shortening the period these companies can charge monopoly prices. Its loss would have been patients' savings.

The bill would have given generic applicants faster certainty on patents and stripped the 180-day exclusivity from first applicants who hoard approvals or sign pay-off deals, so more generics would reach the market sooner alongside cheaper prices for patients.
